full_judgment:
Syed Refaat Ahmed J : This Rule Nisi was issued on 4-11-2018 calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the publication of a separate merit list for Madrasah students in respect of the First Year (Honours) Admission Examinations (2018-2019) of the Faculty of Arts and Humanities (Unit-C) of Jahangirnagar University (Annexures-H(8) & H(9)) and the non-inclusion of the names of Madrasah students in the merit lists prepared by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities of Jahangirnagar University for successful candidates from the 'Science' and 'Humanities' streams in respect of the said Admission Examinations shall not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect, and as to why the Respondents shall not be directed to complete the admission process by incorporating the names of all Madrasah students, including the Petitioners, in the merit list prepared by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities (Unit-C) of Jahangirnagar University for candidates from the 'Science' and 'Humanities' streams and/or such other or further Order or Orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 8. In this Writ Petition, the Petitioner has challenged the legality of the publication of a separate merit list for Madrasah students in respect of the First Year (Honours) Admission Test (2018-2019) of the Faculty of Arts and Humanities of Jahangirnagar University and the non-inclusion of the names of Madrasah students in the merit lists prepared by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities for successful candidates from the 'Science' and 'Humanities' streams of higher secondary education. 

 9. The publication of separate merit lists for different groups of students as categorised by the University authorities (i.e., Humanities/ Science/Commerce/ Madrasah) is directly linked to caps on the number of seats offered to the various groups. This is because Clause 2(Chha) of the Admissions Circular dated 16-8-2018 clearly provides that the number of candidates in the merit list shall be ten times the total number of available seats. Thus, the publication of names of 770 candidates in the Merit List titled 'Male Candidates (Humanities)' indicates that the University authorities has fixed the number of seats available for Male Candidates (Humanities) to 77, while the publication of a separate merit list for 110 Madrasah students indicates that the University authorities has restricted the number of seats available to Madrasah students to only 11. Aggrieved by such caps on the seats being offered to Madrasah students, the Petitioners filed the instant Writ Petition. 

 11. It is noted at the outset that the Rule Nisi that has been issued in the instant Writ Petition is confined to the question of legality of separate classification of Madrasah students. The Petitioner is not aggrieved by nor has he challenged the classification that has been made by the different departments of the Faculty of Arts and Humanities on the basis of the disciplinary backgrounds of the various candidates (i.e., Science/Arts/Commerce). Thus, all questions relating to the legality of such classification as well as the propriety, reasonableness and validity of fixation of a specific number of seats for candidates coming from Science/Arts/Commerce background (i.e., fixing, for instance, the ratio of candidates from Humanities background as 55% and that from Science background as 35% for the Department of International Relations) are beyond the scope of the Rule. 

 12. Given the limited scope of the Rule, the Petitioner's arguments have been confined to the question of legality of separate classification and capping of seats for Madrasah students 

 13. The Petitioner argues that the impugned action of the University in publishing separate merit lists and the capping of seats for Madrasah students is liable to be declared without lawful authority and of no legal effect for the following reasons: 

 (I)	Capping of seats and publication of separate merit lists for Madrasah students not sanctioned by the Jahangirnagar University Act, 1973 ("The Act") and the University Ordinance, 1993 ("The Ordinance"); 

 (II)	Capping of seats and publication of separate merit lists for Madrasah students violate Article 27 of the Constitution; and 

 (III)	Capping of seats and separate merit lists for Madrasah students undermine merit in violation of Clause 7 of the Ordinance. 

 I. Capping of seats and publication of separate merit lists for Madrasah students not sanctioned by law: 

 15. The Petitioner submits that the Act and the Ordinance do not in any manner permit the University authorities to impose any restrictions on the admission of Madrasah students to the University by publishing a separate merit list for Madrasah students and fixing the number of seats available to them, details of which are set out below. 

 17. The constitution and powers of the University Admission Committee (as referred to in section 42 of the Act) are set out in detail in sections 2 and 3 of the Ordinance respectively. Section 3(Ka) of the Ordinance empowers the Admissions Committee to determine the minimum eligibility conditions for admission to the University, while section 3(Ga) of the Ordinance empowers the Admissions Committee to determine the procedure to be adopted by the Departmental Admission Committees for admission of students to the University. In exercise of its powers under section 3 of the Ordinance, the Admissions Committee issued the Admissions Circular dated 16-8-2018 to regulate the admission of students to the University for the Academic Year (2018-2019). Clause 1 of the said Circular contains the minimum eligibility requirements for admission to various departments (as contemplated under section 3(Ka) of the Ordinance), while Clause 2, in particular Clause 2(Chha), of the Circular provides the procedure to be followed by the Departmental Admissions Committee for admission of students to the University (as contemplated under section 3(Ga) of the Ordinance). The Petitioner asserts that no provision of the Circular dated 16-8-2018, as has been issued by the Admissions Committee in exercise of its powers under section 42 of the Act read with section 3 of the Ordinance, allows the capping of seats for Madrasah students and the publication of separate merit lists. As such, the Petitioner submits, the publication of the separate merit list and the capping of seats for Madrasah students by the University's Faculty of Arts and Humanities, being devoid of legal sanction, is liable to be declared without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 II. Capping of seats for Madrasah students and publication of separate merit lists violate Article 27 of the Constitution. 

 19. The Petitioner agitates further that even assuming without conceding that the publication of separate merit lists/capping of seats for Madrasah students is sanctioned by law, such action, being in violation of Article 27 of the Constitution, is liable to be declared without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 21. The Petitioner now contends that having accepted Alim graduates as being at par with candidates who have passed Intermediate examinations, the action of the University in treating Madrasah students as a separate category of students and publishing a separate merit list and capping the number of seats for Madrasah students violates the twin test of equality inherent in Article 27 of the Constitution, i.e., that the classification must be based on 'permissible criteria' or 'intelligible differentia' and that such classification must have a reasonable nexus with the object to be thereby achieved. It is noted that in the case of Sheikh Abdus Sabur vs Returning Officer, reported in 41 DLR (AD) 30, the Appellate Division held in paragraph 29 as follows: 

 It is submitted in this context that Madrasah students being at par with HSC students and having passed the common entrance examinations (where they are tested to the same degree of proficiency and skill) are required to be treated in the same manner as HSC students. Separate classification of Madrasah students in these circumstances is not, therefore, based on any permissible criteria nor does it have any nexus with the object to be achieved of selecting the best candidates for admission to the University. As such, the separate categorisation of Madrasah students violates Article 27 of the Constitution. 

 23. The Petitioner has averred that Alim graduates who have scored much higher in the Admission Examinations (2018-2019) than candidates who have passed Intermediate examinations are being denied a place in the University on account of the cap placed on the number of seats available for Madrasah students. It is pointed out, for instance, the Petitioner who scored a total of 59.425 in the Admission Examinations being an Alim (General) graduate has not been offered a seat in the University's Faculty of Arts and Humanities. However, as many as 32 candidates from the Merit List of 'Male Candidates (Humanities)' (who had passed Intermediate examinations) had been offered seats by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities although they all scored less than the Petitioner in the Admission Examinations. Thus, as a result of the publication of the separate merit lists and the capping of seats for Madrasah students, candidates who are less meritorious are securing admission to the University. As such, the Petitioner argues, the impugned action of the University in restricting admission of Madrasah students undermines merit in violation of Clause 7 of the Ordinance and Clause 2(Chha)(1) of the Circular dated 16-8-2018. 

 24. It is at this juncture that Mr Imran Siddiq has submitted that in view of the fact that the admissions process for the Academic Year 2018-2019 has been completed, the Petitioner did not pray for any Order from this Court which would be tantamount to nullifying the entire admission process. However, since the question of legality of separate merit lists for Madrasah students arises every year, the Petitioner, sought an adjudication by this Court by laying down an authoritative interpretation of Article 27 of the Constitution and section 42 of the Act read with sections 3, 5 and 7 of the Ordinance which will serve as a guidance for the University in subsequent academic years. 

 (i) declaring the publication of separate merit lists for Madrasah students by the Faculty of Arts and Humanities to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and directing that in subsequent academic years the names of Madrasah students be included in the merit lists prepared in respect of candidates from HSC academic background; and 

 32. Ms Mahtab argues that the decision to adopt classifications is an internal administrative policy of the University which should not be interfered with since it has been taken by following rules and without any mala fide intention and for the benefit of all students from different groups. Ms Mahtab stresses further that the classification is purely a 'beneficial classification' since in fact after publication of a separate merit list for male Madrasah students the Petitioner has secured an opportunity to choose either International Relations or Media and Journalism Studies whereas if a combined merit list was published that would not necessarily have been the case and the Petitioner would not get any subject to choose from. Ms Mahtab, accordingly, submits that as the decision of publication of separate merit list for Madrasah students has been taken for the benefit of Madrasah students and has enured to the benefit, for instance, of the Petitioner the Rule Nisi may be found to be without any substance and be discharged. 

 35. In response to the argument of the Respondents that the separate classification of Madrasah students is not hit by Article 27 as it is in the nature of a 'beneficial classification', Mr Siddiq has argued that there is to the contrary ample evidence to show that Madrasah students are being denied admission to the University by virtue of their separate categorisation, although candidates who have scored much less than them are being offered seats at the University. 

 36. Furthermore, as Mr Siddiq points out, for the Academic Year 2018-2019, the University authorities have already determined the various categories of candidates in respect of whom a policy of 'beneficial classification' has been sanctioned, which includes freedom fighters' children, backward and Dalit communities, physically challenged individuals etc. There is a separate application process for admission to the University in such reserved categories. Madrasah students do not fall within any of the aforesaid categories of candidates earmarked by the University by way of 'beneficial classification'. As such, the argument that the separate categorisation of Madrasah students is in the nature of a beneficial classification is found by this Court to be misconceived and flawed. 

 37. Finally, it has aptly been pointed out by the Petitioner that it is only, and curiously so, the Faculty of Arts and Humanities that has resorted to the policy of separate categorisation of Madrasah students. It is difficult for this Court to understand why a policy of 'beneficial classification' for Madrasah students should be pursued by only one Faculty and not uniformly by other Faculties of the University in unison. In other words the true rationale behind this ostensible 'beneficial classification' remains elusive to this Court even notwithstanding the University's insistent invocation of the same. 

 42. Resultantly, the Rule is made absolute-in-part. Accordingly, it is declared that the publication of separate merit lists for Madrasah students by the University's Faculty of Arts and Humanities is without lawful authority and of no legal effect and the University is directed that in subsequent academic years the names of Madrasah students shall be included in the merit lists prepared in respect of candidates from HSC academic backgrounds.
